---
title: "Quiz: 3D images"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Volumes are stored $I[z, y, x]$ with voxel spacing $(\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z)$.

---

**Q1.** A confocal stack has $\Delta x = \Delta y = 0.1$ µm and $\Delta z = 0.4$ µm. A program shows the $xz$ slice with square pixels. What does a round nucleus look like, and why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many rows does the nucleus span in $z$ compared with columns in $x$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Flattened by a factor 4: a nucleus 4 µm across spans 40 columns but only 10 slices, and with square pixels those 10 rows are drawn as tall as 10 columns. The slice must be drawn 4 times taller per row (its physical aspect ratio), or resampled.
:::

---

**Q2.** Voxel $(0, 0, 0)$ is at $(100, 50, 0)$ µm and the spacing is $(0.2, 0.2, 1)$ µm. Where is voxel $(10, 20, 3)$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Start at the origin and step along each axis by index × spacing.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$(100 + 10 \cdot 0.2,\; 50 + 20 \cdot 0.2,\; 0 + 3 \cdot 1) = (102, 54, 3)$ µm.
:::

---

**Q3.** How many voxel values does trilinear interpolation use, and what is the result exactly halfway between all of them?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
The point lies in a cube.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
8 (the corners of the surrounding cube). At the centre every weight is $\tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 \cdot \tfrac12 = \tfrac18$: the mean of the 8 values.
:::

---

**Q4.** To compute an oblique slice, why do we go from each output pixel to the volume, and not from each voxel to the plane?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
How many voxels lie exactly on a tilted plane?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Inverse mapping: every output pixel asks where it comes from and gets one interpolated value. Pushing voxels onto the plane would hit only a few output pixels (almost no voxel lies exactly on the plane), leaving holes. The same reasoning as for rotating a 2D image.
:::

---

**Q5.** You want to smooth a stack with $\Delta x = 0.2$ µm and $\Delta z = 0.6$ µm by the same physical amount in all directions, $\sigma = 0.6$ µm. What $\sigma$ in voxels do you use along $x$ and along $z$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Divide the physical $\sigma$ by the spacing of each axis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$0.6/0.2 = 3$ voxels along $x$ (and $y$), $0.6/0.6 = 1$ voxel along $z$.
:::

---

**Q6.** In a MIP along $z$ you count 12 nuclei. Is the true number at most 12, at least 12, or neither?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What happens to two nuclei at different depths in the projection? Can one nucleus become two?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Usually at least 12: nuclei at different depths that overlap in $x$–$y$ merge into one blob in the MIP, so the projection can only undercount by merging. (A strongly curved cell could in principle appear as two blobs, but that is rare; merging is the common error.) Count in 3D.
:::

---

**Q7.** Does resampling a stack with $\Delta z = 0.5$ µm to isotropic voxels of 0.1 µm improve the resolution along $z$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where do the new values come from?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
No. The new slices are interpolated from the old ones; nothing between the original slices was measured. Resampling makes later steps simpler (cubic voxels, equal neighbourhoods), but costs memory (5 times more voxels here) and adds no detail.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Write the $4 \times 4$ voxel → world matrix for spacing $(0.2, 0.2, 0.5)$ µm and origin $(10, 20, 4)$ µm, and its inverse.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Spacing on the diagonal, origin in the last column; for the inverse, undo the translation, then the scaling.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$$A = \begin{bmatrix} 0.2 & 0 & 0 & 10 \\ 0 & 0.2 & 0 & 20 \\ 0 & 0 & 0.5 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix},\qquad A^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 & 0 & -50 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 & -100 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -8 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$$
:::
